Rider, Cutler, and Mr. Deering upon the business of hemp, then fails to attend the King and Lord Chancellor about navy debts when the meeting fails. Lord Brunkard takes him and Sir Thomas Harvy to the Parke, which is troublesome with dust and has no great beauty but Mrs. Middleton. Mr. Warren proposes Pepys getting L100 to get him a protection for a ship to go out, which Pepys thinks he shall do.

He dined with Navy officers and Ordnance Commissioners at the Dolphin Taverne, where there was good musique at his direction, and their club came to 34s. a man. Afterward he walked alone an hour at Fox-hall observing holiday citizens, then worked late at the office because his wife had not yet returned from being abroad upon the water with his mother, who was to go out of town speedily. He noted that four or five died of the plague in Bell Alley at Westminster on Sunday last, yet people thought the number would be fewer than last week, while the Dutch had come out again with 20 sail under Bankert, supposedly gone northward to meet their East India fleete.

Minnes did expect and intend them a supper, but they without respect to him did first apply themselves to Boreman, which makes all this great feude, and I was forced to go seek a lodging which my W. Hewer did get me.

Returning home, he finds his wife distressed after a falling-out with her maids, particularly Mary, who threatened to reveal something that would "stop her mouth." Suspecting it concerns "Brown," Pepys grows jealous and nearly leaves, but decides to stay, reasoning that the Bezan won't sail till the ebb and that trouble in this sickly plague time could harm the family. He resolves to smooth over the matter, becomes pleasant with his wife, and sleeps content. He ends the month declaring it among the greatest three months of his life for joy, health, and profit, despite the plague season's mortality.
